When piglets nurse from their dead mother, after a brief moment, they look startled and all abandon her and run away. They see that she no longer looks back at them, and that she is no longer like themselves. What they loved in their mother was not her physical body, but that which directed her physical form. When men die in battle, they are buried without their armaments. A man whose feet have been amputated has no reason to care for shoes. In both cases, the foundation is gone.

<margin>Commentary of Su Dongpo <note>Su Shi, 1037–1101, Song dynasty scholar</note></margin> When one does not know the <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> and yet pursues learning, what one hears and sees increases daily; but without a unifying principle to bring them together, this inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, choose what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second tier of knowledge." <note>Analects 7.28</note> If one day one comes to know the Dao and reflects on artificiality and false contrivance, seeing that none of it is anything but illusion, then casting off illusion to return to true nature is called decrease. Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you take me for one who learns widely and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes. Is it not so?" Confucius answered: "No. I hold it together with one thread." <note>Analects 15.3</note> Forgetting the calculating mind in order to purely restore one's true nature may be called decrease; yet illusions may still persist. Only when one forgets even this mind, purely restoring true nature without remainder, can one discard action without losing hold of non-action. People in general possess desires; they wish to manage all worldly affairs and master the world. Therefore they devise undertakings and seek outcomes. When such intent appears outwardly, creatures resent it; hence difficulties arise and nothing can be attained. The sage practices non-action and therefore has no calculating contrivance. When the sage's mind is outwardly revealed, creatures are at peace. Though the sage does not grasp at worldly affairs to manage them, the affairs of the world find natural order and tranquility in him.

<margin>Commentary of Lu Huiqing <note>Song dynasty scholar and official, 1032–1111</note></margin> One who pursues ordinary learning has not yet heard the Dao. Not having heard the Dao, in seeking it one cannot help but become broad and encyclopedic; hence it is said, "one gains daily." One who cultivates the Dao has already heard the Dao. Having heard the Dao, in practicing it one cannot help but remain in <term>wuwei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss>; hence it is said, "one decreases daily." To decrease and further decrease still falls short of avoiding conscious effort entirely; only when one decreases even the very act of decreasing does one finally arrive at non-action. Non-action means silent stillness, untouched by agitation. Having nothing left undone means being moved and thereby penetrating all affairs beneath Heaven. Proceeding through non-action to reach consummate non-action is what is called the constant standard. To pursue learning without anxiety is called spiritual wonder. The spiritual wonder becoming an orderly method is what is called the Dao. As for this ultimate spiritual state, who could possibly equal it? Viewed from this perspective, winning the world is constantly achieved through non-action; when relying on calculated effort, it is insufficient to win the world, as one may readily know.

<margin>Commentary of Huang Maocai <note>Song dynasty commentator</note></margin> Only after there is nothing one does not know can one truly speak of learning; therefore, learning seeks daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one truly speak of the Dao; therefore, the Dao seeks daily decrease. However, what increases can be pursued forward, while what decreases may be difficult to force into being. Only one of supreme illumination can in a sudden flash drop everything away, thereby reaching the realm of non-action. Thus, such a one leaves nothing undone, applies it without exhaustion, and extends it throughout the world with great ease and abundance.

<margin>Commentary of Xizhai <note>Commentator identity associated with the Daoist lineage</note></margin> The pursuit of learning is for seeking knowledge, hence daily increase; the cultivation of the Dao is for expelling delusion, hence daily decrease. If knowledge is not thorough, reduction cannot be complete; therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is removed and authenticity is made whole, one reaches non-action. Arriving at non-action, whatever deliberate action exists is never without non-action; this again cannot be readily measured by increase and decrease. When non-action reaches its culmination, though the affairs of the world be myriad, one unifies them with a single thread. If one takes contrivance to breed more contrivance, it becomes difficult to find rest; even a single matter before oneself remains entangled and contradictory, not to mention the immense multiplicity of the world.

The sage has no constant mind of his own, but takes the mind of the common people as his mind. Those who are good I treat with goodness; those who are not good I also treat with goodness; thus virtue is goodness. Those who are trustworthy I trust; those who are untrustworthy I also trust; thus virtue is trust. The sage in the world is self-effacing and modest, and for the sake of the world makes his mind merged and undivided. The common people all fix their ears and eyes upon him; the sage

"Yesterday I had criticisms of you, but today my mind has turned back and abandoned them. What is the reason for this?"

Laozi said: "As for those people endowed with clever wisdom and divine sagacity, I consider myself to have cast off such things. In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had one thousand officers, while the feudal lords had one hundred officers. By means of these one thousand officers, having one's commands executed throughout the states of the Central Lands <note>original: "諸夏" (Zhu Xia), referring to the Chinese realm</note> is called being a true king <note>original: "王" (wang)</note>. By means of these one hundred officers, having one's commands executed within one's borders, so that although the state may face instability it does not reach the point of deposition, replacement, and total ruin <gloss>annotator note: read <term>sui</term> <gloss>遂</gloss> as <term>zhui</term> <gloss>墜, to fall or ruin</gloss>, meaning to abandon one's inherited heritage</gloss>, is called being a ruler <note>original: "君" (jun)</note>. 

Now consider the son of a sage king: he succeeds to the possessor of all under Heaven, he holds the ancestral registers of lineage, and he belongs to the premier clan of all under Heaven. Yet if he is untalented and not upright <gloss>annotator note: <term>bu zhong</term> <gloss>不中</gloss> means not balanced and upright</gloss>, internally the common people will detest him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those near at hand within his borders will not be unified, while those far away among the feudal lords will not obey. His commands will not take effect even within his own borders, and in extreme cases, the feudal lords will encroach upon him, diminish his lands, attack him, and chastise him. In such circumstances, although he has not yet perished outright, I say that he no longer possesses all under Heaven.

When a sage king passes away and the successor holding the royal registers is feeble, weak, and unable to govern or bind <gloss>annotator note: <term>ba</term> <gloss>罷</gloss> is pronounced <term>pi</term> <gloss>ㄆㄧ</gloss>, meaning feeble and incapable of duty; <term>xian</term> <gloss>縣</gloss> means <term>xi</term> <gloss>繫, to attach or hold together</gloss> all under Heaven together, then all under Heaven is left without a true ruler. If among the feudal lords there is one whose bright virtue and accumulated majesty inspire all people within the seas to wish to have him as their lord and teacher, and yet a tyrannical state acts with insolence and unchecked license, then how could he punish them? <gloss>annotator note: tyrannical states refer to realms like those of Jie and Zhou; <term>du chi</term> <gloss>獨侈</gloss> means unrestrained indulgence; <term>an</term> <gloss>安</gloss> is used in the sense of "then"</gloss> He will certainly not harm innocent people. He executes the ruler of a tyrannical state just as if executing a solitary tyrant who stands completely abandoned <gloss>annotator note: <term>du fu</term> <gloss>獨夫</gloss> means one whom nobody under Heaven supports, standing entirely as a lone individual</gloss>. </gloss>

When matters are handled in this manner, such a ruler can be called one capable of employing all under Heaven. Being capable of employing all under Heaven is what is called being a true king. Tang and Wu did not seize all under Heaven by force. They cultivated their moral Way, practiced their righteousness, shared common benefits with all under Heaven, and eliminated common harms for all under Heaven, and therefore all under Heaven turned to them. Jie and Zhou did not have all under Heaven stripped away from them by others. They inverted the virtue of Yu and Tang, threw into disorder the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, acted like beasts, accumulated their own calamities, and brought destruction upon what was beneath them <gloss>annotator note: this means that all under Heaven naturally departed from them on its own</gloss>.

<summary>Xunzi defines true kingship versus mere lordship through moral authority and service to the realm, demonstrating that monarchs like Tang and Wu received the world voluntarily while tyrants like Jie and Zhou lost it through their own depravity.</summary>

### 3. Revealing the Characteristics of the Above Dependent Origination
This refers to the phrase "there are defiled minds."

#### First, Marking the Topic
"Defiled minds are of six kinds."

#### Second, Inquiring
"What are the six?"
Within the six, each has two parts: first the obstacle, and second the remedy.

#### Third, Explaining
Now these six defilements correspond in reverse order to the first four of the six coarse aspects and the last three of the subtle aspects. Because *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Fascicle One, same as above,
this first combines the third and fourth among those coarse aspects, there are only six. It simply borrows these names to categorize these six.

#### First, the Aspect of Grasping and Reckoning Names
"First is defilement associated with grasping, because it is distanced from by relying on the liberation of the two vehicles and the stage of faith correspondence." This is the third and fourth aspects among the six coarse aspects. It is also the meaning of what is augmented by the afflictions of views and attachment in the active mental consciousness above. It is also the aspect of discriminating and clinging in the four phases above. But the coarse mind outwardly grasps and corresponds with objects, defiling its pure practice; hence it is called "defiled." In the liberation of the two vehicles, upon reaching the stage of non-learning, the afflictions of view and cultivation are completely abandoned. Those of "faith correspondence" refer to those from the ten understandings onward, whose roots of faith are perfected without regression; hence it is called "faith correspondence." Therefore, the *Treatise on the Ten Stages* <note>original: "地論"</note> says: "Before the stages, all are called Bodhisattvas of the stage of faith practice." Asanga's treatise also agrees with this statement. This Bodhisattva

<column-break/>

attains the emptiness of persons, so that afflictions of view and cultivation cannot arise actively. Hence it says "distanced from." It is not said in terms of dormant tendencies, because afflictions are intentionally retained. As the *Compendium of the Mahayana* <note>original: "攝論"</note> says: "If one does not sever the active mind, one does not differ from ordinary beings; if one does not retain the seeds of affliction, one does not differ from the two vehicles." Furthermore, there are two intentions in retaining afflictions: for oneself and for others. This is stated according to the final teaching. If stated according to the initial teaching, retaining afflictions is only spoken of from the first stage and above, as stated in other treatises. Now this Bodhisattva not only severs the attachment to persons of the four active stations, but also partially severs the ground of ignorance dwelling. Therefore later in this treatise it says: "One who does not understand the meaning of the one realm of reality" is observed and learned to be severed from the stage of faith correspondence. Now it only reveals the coarse aspect of selfhood of persons, hence it does not discuss that.

#### Second, the Aspect of Continuity
"Second is defilement associated with non-interruption, because one gradually abandons it by cultivating skillful means on the stage of faith correspondence, and completely leaves it behind upon attaining the stage of a pure mind."
*Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Fascicle One, same as above.
This is the second among the six coarse aspects. From this up to the sixth, they again correspond in reverse order to the former five minds. This position is the fifth. Simply grasping dharmas in continuous rebirth, arising continuously without interruption: this is the meaning of continuity. From the ten understandings onward, through the skillful means of reflection and investigation in the contemplation of mere-consciousness, up to the first stage where one realizes the three non-natures and pervasive true suchness, the discrimination of dharma-grasping cannot actively arise.
